title: Liquidity and working capital
goal: Calculate and interpret current, quick, and cash ratios without assuming a universal ideal value.

slides.title: Can the business meet its near-term obligations?

items.heading: Resources
items.text: Cash and assets expected to be realized or used soon.

items.heading: Obligations
items.text: Supplier bills, customer services owed, and current loan principal.

slides.takeaway: Liquidity is about amounts and timing.
slides.notes: A customer advance may be settled by providing services rather than paying cash.

slides.title: Working capital compares current assets and liabilities

blocks.text: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

slides.takeaway: Working capital is a dollar amount, not a cash balance.
slides.notes: Current liabilities include $6,000 of note principal. Inventory and prepaid insurance are not cash available today.

slides.title: Calculate the current ratio
slides.takeaway: $1.56 of current assets per $1 of current liabilities.
slides.notes: Round final results only. A ratio above one does not guarantee payment on time. There is no universal ideal across industries.

slides.title: Identify which assets belong in the quick ratio
slides.takeaway: Subtracting inventory alone would leave prepaid insurance in the numerator.
slides.notes: No investments or receivable allowance in this case. Use qualifying net receivables in fuller datasets.

slides.title: Calculate the cash ratio
slides.takeaway: This course uses cash and cash equivalents in the numerator.
slides.notes: Some references also include marketable securities. State the convention before comparing. The case has neither cash equivalents nor such securities.

slides.title: Use one balance sheet to compare all three ratios
slides.takeaway: All three use current liabilities of $8,100.
slides.notes: Current to quick excludes Inventory $2,200 and Prepaid Insurance $600. Quick to cash excludes Receivables $1,000.

slides.title: A stronger ratio can still hide a cash problem

items: Receivables may be overdue or disputed.
Debt payments may fall due before customer collections.

slides.takeaway: Read ratios beside cash flows and account details.
slides.notes: A high ratio can reflect excess inventory or slow collections. Business models and payment timing affect interpretation.

slides.title: Try it: explain a liquidity change

blocks.text: Summit Trail pays $600 of Accounts Payable immediately after June 30.

slides.lead: What happens to cash and the current ratio?
slides.takeaway: The current ratio rises even though cash falls.
slides.notes: Hypothetical subsequent event, not an extra June transaction. Nothing else changes.

slides.title: Choose a useful comparison and state a limitation

items.heading: Compare
items.text: Use prior periods and similar businesses.

items.heading: Explain
items.text: Name the accounts driving the change.

slides.lead: What evidence would you request before recommending another loan?
slides.notes: Supports the year-end report. Avoid universal healthy thresholds and “higher is always better.”

blocks.text: Request a cash forecast, customer collection history, and debt payment schedule. Explain how each affects the ability to pay.
